title: Benvenuti! Welcome to Italian
topics: What Italian is, the family it belongs to, and why it is worth learning

explain: You are about to learn a language spoken by around 65 million people as their mother tongue, and by many millions more who learned it for love, work or family. It is the language of Dante and Verdi, of pizza and espresso, and of half the words written on a music score. The good news: it is also one of the friendliest languages to start with.

explain.caption: The five biggest Romance languages in Europe, in the countries where each one is the main language.

explain: Italian belongs to the Romance family: the languages that grew out of Latin, the language of ancient Rome. As the Roman Empire spread, so did Latin, and over the centuries it slowly turned into different languages in different places. Italian’s closest relatives are Spanish, Portuguese, French, Catalan and Romanian. Of the big Romance languages, Italian is often said to have stayed closest to Latin.
You can see the family resemblance at a glance:

note: English is not a Romance language, but it took thousands of words from Latin and French. That is why *notte* feels close to “nocturnal”, *mano* to “manual” and *acqua* to “aquarium”: you already know more Italian than you think.

explain: If you already speak Spanish, French or another Romance language, Italian will often feel like a cousin you are meeting for the first time: different, but strangely familiar.

Italian is the official language of Italy and San Marino, one of the four national languages of Switzerland, and one of the languages of Vatican City. It is also spoken in parts of Slovenia and Croatia, and by large communities whose families emigrated to Argentina, Brazil, the United States, Canada and Australia.

explain.picture: A map of Italy with Florence marked, and Switzerland, San Marino and Vatican City shown around it

explain.h: From Florence to the whole country

explain: For centuries every Italian region spoke its own dialect, and many still do. Standard Italian grew out of the language of Florence, thanks to three Tuscan writers of the 1300s: Dante, Petrarch and Boccaccio. Dante’s *Divina Commedia* became so famous that his Florentine became the model for writers everywhere. When Italy became one country in 1861, only a small part of its people spoke Italian every day. School, newspapers, radio and television did the rest.

explain.h: Why Italian is a good place to start

ul: You read it as you write it. Italian spelling is very regular: once you know a few rules (the next lesson shows them), you can read any word aloud.
Many words look familiar. Thanks to Latin, words like *università*, *famiglia*, *musica* or *importante* need almost no explanation.
It opens a whole culture. Opera, film, design, fashion, food, art and history: in Italian you meet them first-hand.
It is a door to other languages. After Italian, Spanish, Portuguese and French become much easier.
It is useful. Italy is a major destination for travel, study and business, and Italian is one of the languages people around the world most like to learn.

explain: Each lesson has the same parts: an explanation, practice, new words, a text to read, a dialogue to listen to, and a writing task. This first lesson and the next one are in English, to help you settle in. From lesson 3 everything is in Italian, simple at first. Point at an Italian word to see what it means.

text.picture: The red and gold hall of La Scala opera house in Milan, seen from the stage

text: Open any music score and you are reading Italian: *piano*, *forte*, *allegro*, *adagio*, *crescendo*. Around the year 1000 a monk from Arezzo, Guido, gave the notes the names we still sing as do-re-mi. Opera was born in Italy around 1600, and the operas of Verdi, Puccini and Rossini still fill theatres from Milan to Tokyo. Every February the whole country watches the same song festival: Sanremo, held since 1951.

text.picture: Michelangelo’s statue of David in Florence, seen from below

text: In the 1400s Florence started something that changed Europe: the Renaissance. Painters, sculptors and architects such as Botticelli, Leonardo da Vinci, Michelangelo and Raphael looked back to ancient Rome and Greece and found new ways of seeing the world. Today Italy is among the countries with the most UNESCO World Heritage Sites, and in many Italian towns you walk through history on your way to buy bread.

text.picture: A wooden table with fresh pasta, tomatoes, basil, olive oil and a small cup of espresso

text: Italians often say there is no single “Italian cooking”, only the cooking of each region: butter and rice in the north, olive oil and tomatoes in the south, and a different pasta shape almost everywhere. A meal is a time to sit down together, and Italians talk about food with real passion. The art of the Neapolitan pizza maker is even on UNESCO’s list of the world’s living heritage.

text.picture: The Colosseum in Rome at sunset

text: Rome was once the centre of an empire that reached from Britain to Egypt, and Latin travelled with it. Much later, cities such as Venice, Genoa and Florence grew rich through trade and banking, and Marco Polo set off from Venice for China. For a long time Italy was divided into many small states. It became one kingdom in 1861, and on 2 June 1946 Italians voted to become a republic, a day the country still celebrates every year.
